verses.zh: 希西家王听见就撕裂衣服，披上麻布，进了耶和华的殿，
verses.en: When King Hezekiah heard this,[NOTE:1] he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and went to the Lord’s temple.
notes: The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.
verses.commentary:
37:1 "he tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth" These are signs of mourning.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

▣ "the house of the Lord" This refers to the temple in Jerusalem. Exactly
what area of the temple he entered is uncertain. Only priests and Levites had access to the sacred buildings.
However, there was a special area set aside for the monarch to be as close as possible and view the activities
of festival rituals.

verses.zh: 使家宰以利亚敬和书记舍伯那，并祭司中的长老，都披上麻布，去见亚摩斯的儿子先知以赛亚，
verses.en: Eliakim the palace supervisor, Shebna the scribe, and the leading priests,[NOTE:1] clothed in sackcloth, sent this message to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz:
notes: Heb “elders of the priests” (so KJV, NAB, NASB); NCV “the older priests”; NRSV, TEV, CEV “the senior priests.”
verses.commentary: 37:2 "Eliakim. . .Shebna" See note at Isa. 36:3,22.

verses.zh: 对他说：「希西家如此说：『今日是急难、责罚、凌辱的日子，就如妇人将要生产婴孩，却没有力量生产。
verses.en: “This is what Hezekiah says:[NOTE:1] ‘This is a day of distress, insults,[NOTE:2] and humiliation,[NOTE:3] as when a baby is ready to leave the birth canal but the mother lacks the strength to push it through.[NOTE:4]
notes: In the Hebrew text this verse begins with “they said to him” (cf. NRSV).
Or “rebuke” (KJV, NAB, NIV, NRSV), or “correction.”
Or “contempt”; NAB, NIV, NRSV “disgrace.”
Heb “when sons come to the cervical opening and there is no strength to give birth.”
verses.commentary:
37:3 Hezekiah vividly describes the situation (cf. 2 Kgs. 19:3).

- NASB, NRSV ‒ "a day of distress" (BDB 865 I)

NKJV ‒ "a day of trouble"

NJB ‒ "a day of suffering"

LXX ‒ "a day of affliction"

- NASB, NKJV, NRSV, "a day of rebuke" (BDB 407)

NJB ‒ "a day of punishment"

LXX ‒ "a day of reproach"

- NASB ‒ "a day of rejection" (BDB 611)

NKJV ‒ "a day of blasphemy"

NRSV, NJB ‒ "a day of disgrace"

"a day of rebuke"

- LXX, Peshitta, "a day of anger"

- "time for birth, but no strength to deliver"

All of these phrases refer to YHWH's actions, not Assyria's. Hezekiah knew the problem was covenant
disobedience and faithlessness. Assyria was not the real problem, but YHWH's instrument of judgment against a
disobedient covenant people (i.e. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28).

verses.zh: 或者耶和华―你的　神听见拉伯沙基的话，就是他主人亚述王打发他来辱骂永生　神的话；耶和华―你的　神听见这话就发斥责。故此，求你为余剩的民扬声祷告。』」
verses.en: Perhaps the Lord your God will hear all these things the chief adviser has spoken on behalf of his master, the king of Assyria, who sent him to taunt the living God.[NOTE:1] When the Lord your God hears, perhaps he will punish him for the things he has said.[NOTE:2] So pray for this remnant that remains.’”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “all the words of the chief adviser whom his master, the king of Assyria, sent to taunt the living God.”
Heb “and rebuke the words which the Lord your God hears.”
Heb “and lift up a prayer on behalf of the remnant that is found.”
verses.commentary:
37:4 Hezekiah is hoping that as YHWH heard the blasphemy (i.e. "reproach," BDB 357,
KB 355, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, cf. Isa. 37:17,23,24) of
Assyria's arrogant boast (cf. Isa. 36:15,18,20), He would defend His name (i.e. Ezek. 36:22-23).

▣ "the remnant" This term can be used in several senses depending on the context.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT, Three Senses

verses.zh: 希西家王的臣仆就去见以赛亚。
verses.en: When King Hezekiah’s servants came to Isaiah,

verses.zh: 以赛亚对他们说：「要这样对你们的主人说，耶和华如此说：『你听见亚述王的仆人亵渎我的话，不要惧怕。
verses.en: Isaiah said to them, “Tell your master this: ‘This is what the Lord has said: “Don’t be afraid because of the things you have heard—these insults the king of Assyria’s servants have hurled against me.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “by which the servants of the king of Assyria have insulted me.”

verses.zh: 我必惊动（原文是使灵进入）他的心；他要听见风声就归回本地，我必使他在那里倒在刀下。』」
verses.en: Look, I will take control of his mind;[NOTE:1] he will receive a report and return to his own land. I will cut him down[NOTE:2] with a sword in his own land.”’”
notes: Heb “I will put in him a spirit.” The precise sense of רוּחַ (ruakh, “spirit”) is uncertain in this context. It may refer to a spiritual being who will take control of his mind (see 1 Kgs 22:19), or it could refer to a disposition of concern and fear. In either case the Lord’s sovereignty over the king is apparent.
Heb “cause him to fall” (so KJV, ASV, NAB), that is, “kill him.”
verses.commentary:
37:7

NASB, NJB, LXX
"I will put a spirit in him"

NKJV
"I will send a spirit upon him"

NRSV
"I myself will put a spirit in him"

TEV
"The Lord will cause the emperor to hear"

REB
"I shall sap his morale"

Peshitta
"I will send a blast against him"

JPSOA
"I will delude him"

The MT has ruah (BDB 924), which, in this context, refers to an inner feeling or
sense of doom and foreboding. The "great king"of Assyria (cf. Isa. 36:4) is controlled by the God of Israel!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

▣ "hear a rumor and return to his own land" This is YHWH's response because Hezekiah turned to Him
for help (as Ahaz did not). He will confuse the army and send them home (cf. Isa. 37:37). Some have wondered
if Isa. 37:9 is not a fulfillment of this rumor, but it seems, in context, to refer to a rumor that will
force him to return to Assyria and not simply meet Egypt in battle.

▣ "I will make him fall by the sword in his own land" See Isa. 37:38 for the historical fulfillment
of this prophecy.

verses.zh: 拉伯沙基回去，正遇见亚述王攻打立拿；原来他早听见亚述王拔营离开拉吉。
verses.en: When the chief adviser heard the king of Assyria had departed from Lachish, he left and went to Libnah, where the king was campaigning.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and the chief adviser returned and he found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he heard that he had departed from Lachish.”

verses.zh: 亚述王听见人论古实王特哈加说：「他出来要与你争战。」亚述王一听见，就打发使者去见希西家，吩咐他们说：
verses.en: The king[NOTE:1] heard that King Tirhakah of Ethiopia[NOTE:2] was marching out to fight him.[NOTE:3] He again sent[NOTE:4] messengers to Hezekiah, ordering them:
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (the king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “Cush” (so NASB, NIV11); NIV84, NCV “the Cushite king of Egypt.”
Heb “heard concerning Tirhakah king of Cush, ‘He has come out to fight with you.’”
The Hebrew text has, “and he heard and he sent,” but the parallel in 2 Kgs 19:9 has וַיָּשָׁב וַיִּשְׁלַח (vayyashav vayyishlakh, “and he returned and he sent”), i.e., “he again sent.”
verses.commentary:
37:9-11 This repeats Isa. 36:13-20.

37:9 "Tirhakah king of Cush" There have been some historical problems connected with this verse because
this man, though the younger brother of the current Pharaoh of Egypt (i.e. twenty-fifth Nubian Dynasty),
Shebitku, nephew of Shabaka, possibly reigned from 696/95 ‒ 685/84 B.C. (?)
Tirhakah became a Pharaoh and reigned from 690 ‒ 664 B.C. He was also known
as the King of Ethiopia (cf. 2 Kgs. 19:9). However, this may be a military title or an anachronism
(which means that one reads a later event or person into an earlier document). Hence, in this text,
Tirhakah was only Pharaoh's representative sent with the army.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF EGYPT

verses.zh: 「你们对犹大王希西家如此说：『不要听你所倚靠的　神欺哄你说：耶路撒冷必不交在亚述王的手中。
verses.en: “Tell King Hezekiah of Judah this: ‘Don’t let your God in whom you trust mislead you when he says, “Jerusalem will not be handed over to the king of Assyria.”

verses.zh: 你总听说亚述诸王向列国所行的乃是尽行灭绝，难道你还能得救吗？
verses.en: Certainly you have heard how the kings of Assyria have annihilated all lands.[NOTE:1] Do you really think you will be rescued?[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Look, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the lands, annihilating them.”
Heb “and will you be rescued?” The rhetorical question expects the answer, “No, of course not!”

verses.zh: 我列祖所毁灭的，就是歌散、哈兰、利色，和属提・拉撒的伊甸人；这些国的神何曾拯救这些国呢？
verses.en: Were the nations whom my predecessors[NOTE:1] destroyed—the nations of Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden in Telassar—rescued by their gods?[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “fathers” (so KJV, NAB, NASB); NIV84 “forefathers”; NIV11 “predecessors”; NCV “ancestors.”
Heb “Did the gods of the nations whom my fathers destroyed rescue them—Gozan and Haran, and Rezeph and the sons of Eden who are in Telassar?”
verses.commentary:
37:12-13 There are several geographical locations mentioned that Assyria had previously conquered.

- Gozan ‒ In 2 Kgs. 17:6; 18:11; 1 Chr. 5:26 this is called a river (i.e. region) of Mesopotamia
where Tiglath-pileser III exiled people from the tribal areas of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh, and later,
more of the northern ten tribes by Sargon II.

- Haran ‒ This was a city in Assyria (cf. Gen. 12:4; 24:4) that had rebelled and was destroyed
by Asshur-dan III in 763 B.C.

- Rezeph ‒ This is another significant city in Assyria, conquered by Shalmanezer III
(858 ‒ 824 B.C.). It may have been conquered several times, but
information is minimal.

- Telassar ‒ This is a city or kingdom of Eden which was conquered by Tiglath-pileser III. It
was close to the border of Elam.

- Hamath ‒ This is a city in Syria on the border with Israel. Some of its citizens were
exiled into Israel.

- Arpad ‒ This is a city in northern Syria, the capital of a province or small kingdom (Bit-Agusi).
It was defeated by Tiglath-pileser III in 740 B.C.

- Lair ‒ This is a city of northern Babylon whose spelling is close to "city"
(BDB 746, ריע, NJB, NET Bible).

- Sepharvaim ‒ See note at Isa. 36:19

- Hena ‒ This is a city possibly in upper Mesopotamia (cf. ABD, vol. 3, p. 137).

- Ivvah ‒ This is an unknown locality. Some scholars associate #8 and #9 with the name of local gods.

The purpose of mentioning these specific cities (which Hezekiah must have known or which were on the
way from Assyria to Palestine which Sennacherib conquered) was to show that no one could resist the
Assyrian military!

verses.zh: 哈马的王，亚珥拔的王，西法瓦音城的王，希拿和以瓦的王，都在哪里呢？』」
verses.en: Where is the king of Hamath or the king of Arpad or the kings of Lair,[NOTE:1] Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?’”
notes: Lair was a city located in northeastern Babylon. See M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 235.

verses.zh: 希西家从使者手里接过书信来，看完了，就上耶和华的殿，将书信在耶和华面前展开。
verses.en: Hezekiah took the letter[NOTE:1] from the messengers and read it.[NOTE:2] Then Hezekiah went up to the Lord’s temple and spread it out before the Lord.
notes: The Hebrew text has the plural, “letters.” The final mem (ם) may be dittographic (note the initial mem on the form that immediately follows). Some Greek and Aramaic witnesses have the singular. If so, one still has to deal with the yod that is part of the plural ending. J. N. Oswalt refers to various commentators who have suggested ways to understand the plural form (Isaiah [NICOT], 1:652).
In the parallel text in 2 Kgs 19:14 the verb has the plural suffix, “them,” but this may reflect a later harmonization to the preceding textual reading of “letters.”
verses.commentary:
37:14 This is obviously firsthand detailed historical narrative. It is very graphic and specific. Readers
can see in their minds Hezekiah approaching YHWH, somewhere in the temple compound (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:33),
unscrolling these Assyrian messages before Him so that He could read them. Hezekiah mentions in Isa. 37:4
that YHWH heard Rabshakeh read the message from the King of Assyria. Hezekiah now wants to remind Him
of their arrogant and blasphemous character!

verses.zh: 希西家向耶和华祷告说：
verses.en: Hezekiah prayed before the Lord:

verses.zh: 「坐在二基路伯上万军之耶和华―以色列的　神啊，你―惟有你是天下万国的　神，你曾创造天地。
verses.en: “O Lord of Heaven’s Armies, O God of Israel, who is enthroned on the cherubim![NOTE:1] You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the sky[NOTE:2] and the earth.
notes: The cherubim (singular “cherub”) refer to the images of winged angelic creatures that were above the ark of the covenant.
Or “the heavens.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heavens” or “sky” depending on the context.
verses.commentary:
37:16 Notice the titles and ways Hezekiah characterizes YHWH.

- O Lord of hosts (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts)

- the God (Elohim) of Israel, cf. Josh. 7:13,19,20 (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.)

- who is enthroned above the cherubim, cf. Exod. 25:22; 1 Sam. 4:4; 2 Sam. 6:2; 2 Kgs. 19:15;
1 Chr. 13:6; Ps. 80:1; 99:1
(SPECIAL TOPIC: CHERUBIM and SPECIAL TOPIC: ARK OF THE COVENANT)

- You are the God (Elohim), cf. Deut. 10:17

- You alone, this term (BDB 94) is denoting monotheism here and YHWH's choice of Israel as His
instrument of redemption for all the world
(
SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM)

- You have made heaven and earth, 42:5; 45:18; Gen. 1:1

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，求你侧耳而听；耶和华啊，求你睁眼而看，要听西拿基立的一切话，他是打发使者来辱骂永生　神的。
verses.en: Pay attention, Lord, and hear! Open your eyes, Lord, and observe! Listen to this entire message Sennacherib sent and how he taunts the living God![NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “Hear all the words of Sennacherib which he sent to taunt the living God.”
verses.commentary:
37:17 There is a series of IMPERATIVES in Hezekiah's prayer used as reverent
requests.

- incline Your ear, BDB 639, KB 692, Hiphil IMPERATIVE,
cf. Dan. 9:18

- hear, BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE

- open Your eyes, BDB 824, KB 959, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Dan. 9:18

- see, BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE

- listen, same as #2

Hezekiah is using anthropomorphic language (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN) to beseech God to hear, see, and respond
to the arrogant, blasphemous message of Sennacherib.

These same VERBS are used in Solomon's dedication of the temple
in 1 Kgs. 8:29,52; 2 Chr. 6:39-40; 7:15.

▣ "the living God" This verse is very anthropomorphic (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE), attributing to
YHWH human body parts as if He were a man. The OT presents God as an eternal, ever-present
spirit. The term "living God" is a play on the name YHWH from Exod. 3:14, which means "I Am that I Am."

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，亚述诸王果然使列国和列国之地变为荒凉，
verses.en: It is true, Lord, that the kings of Assyria have destroyed all the nations[NOTE:1] and their lands.
notes: The Hebrew text here has “all the lands,” but the parallel text in 2 Kgs 19:17 has “the nations.”
verses.commentary: 37:18 There was surely a measure of truth in Sennacherib's claims.

verses.zh: 将列国的神像都扔在火里；因为他本不是神，乃是人手所造的，是木头、石头的，所以灭绝他。
verses.en: They have burned the gods of the nations,[NOTE:1] for they are not really gods, but only the product of human hands manufactured from wood and stone. That is why the Assyrians could destroy them.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and they put their gods in the fire.”
Heb “so they destroyed them” (NASB similar).
verses.commentary:
37:19 The truth of Isa. 37:18 is seen to be overstated because the gods of the cities mentioned were
idols, not the true and only God! Idols were made by human hands. They could not see and hear and respond
(i.e. Isa. 37:17) as YHWH could, would, and will!

verses.zh: 耶和华―我们的　神啊，现在求你救我们脱离亚述王的手，使天下万国都知道惟有你是耶和华。」
verses.en: Now, O Lord our God, rescue us from his power, so all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the Lord.”[NOTE:1]
notes: The parallel text in 2 Kgs 19:19 reads, “that you, Lord, are the only God.”
verses.commentary:
37:20 This verse has two VERBS.

- deliver, BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil IMPERATIVE,
cf. Isa. 25:9; 33:22; 35:4. It is used fourteen times in chapters 40-66.

- know, BDB 393, KB 390, Qal IMPERFECT used in
a JUSSIVE sense (

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW)

This is a very important verse and shows the ultimate purpose of YHWH's acts. Israel was meant
to be a kingdom of priests (cf. Exod. 19:5-6). From the initial call of Abraham (cf. Gen. 12:3), God's plan
was to deal with the entire world (cf. Isa. 2:2-4; 12:4-5; 25:6-9; 42:6,10-12; 45:8,22; 49:5-6; 51:4-5; 60:1-3; 66:18,23).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "that You alone, Lord, are God" This is surely an affirmation of
the uniqueness of Israel's God in the ancient world. He was God alone. There was no other (cf. Isa. 43:11;
45:5,18,21-22). This is the theological affirmation of monotheism!

The phrase "art God" is not in the MT, but is in the DSS, LXX, and the parallel in 2 Kgs. 19:19.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

verses.zh: 亚摩斯的儿子以赛亚就打发人去见希西家，说：「耶和华―以色列的　神如此说，你既然求我攻击亚述王西拿基立，
verses.en: Isaiah son of Amoz sent this message to Hezekiah: “This is what the Lord God of Israel has said: ‘As to what you have prayed to me concerning King Sennacherib of Assyria,[NOTE:1]
notes: The parallel text in 2 Kgs 19:20 includes a verb, “What you have prayed … I have heard.”
verses.commentary:
37:21-24 This is YHWH's response to Hezekiah's faith and the resulting message to Assyria, who went
beyond YHWH's purpose (cf. Isa. 10:5) and became arrogant and blasphemous.

- Isa. 37:22, she despised (BDB 100, KB 114, Qal PERFECT),
mocked (BDB 541, KB 532, Qal PERFECT), and shook her
head at (BDB 631, KB 681, Hiphil PERFECT) Judah, here called

- the virgin daughter of Zion

- the daughter of Jerusalem

- The Peshitta, TEV, and REB see Isa. 37:22 as referring to Judah's actions toward retreating
Sennacherib, but I think it refers to Assyria's arrogance against Judah that YHWH is reacting
to. The question is who does "she" refer to. Sennacherib is the "him" of Isa. 37:22a, but
"she" could refer to

- Assyria

- Judah

- Isa. 37:23, she attacked Judah's God (i.e. the Holy One of Israel)

- reproached, BDB 357, KB 355, Piel PERFECT

- blasphemed, BDB 154, KB 180, Piel PERFECT

- raised your voice, BDB 926, KB 1202, Hiphil PERFECT

- haughtily lifted your eyes, BDB 669, KB 724, Qal IMPERFECT with
waw, cf. Isa. 10:12

- Isa. 37:24, lauds her activities

- with many chariots I came up to the heights of the mountains, to the remotest parts
of Lebanon

- cut down its tall cedars and choicest cypresses (Isaiah used many allusions to trees)

- I will go to its highest peak, its thickest forest

Isaiah 37:24 is similar to the arrogance of the King of Babylon (that I think refers to
Merodach-baladan, cf. Isa. 39:1), mentioned in Isa. 14:13. If so, then possibly the language here also
refers to the northern mountain of the gods of Canaanite mythology, see note at Isa. 14:13-14.

37:21 "Because you have prayed to Me" Hezekiah responds in faith and trust in YHWH, so different
from his father, Ahaz. This shows the theological significance of intercessory prayer. I believe that
God has limited Himself to act in response to the prayers of His children. Therefore, we have not
because we ask not (i.e. James 4:2).

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

verses.zh: 所以耶和华论他这样说：锡安的处女藐视你，嗤笑你；耶路撒冷的女子向你摇头。
verses.en: this is what the Lord says about him:[NOTE:1] “‘The virgin daughter Zion[NOTE:2] despises you—she makes fun of you;daughter Jerusalem shakes her head after you.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “this is the word which the Lord has spoken about him.”

Zion (Jerusalem) is pictured here as a young, vulnerable daughter whose purity is being threatened by the would-be Assyrian rapist. The personification hints at the reality which the young girls of the city would face if the Assyrians conquered it.
Shaking the head was a mocking gesture of derision.
verses.commentary:
37:22 "She has shaken her head behind you" This VERB (BDB 631,
KB 681, Hiphil PERFECT) denotes a Hebrew idiom of shaking one's head
as a sign of contempt (cf. 2 Kgs. 19:21; Job 16:4; Ps. 22:7; 109:25; Lam. 2:15; Matt. 27:39; Mark 15:29).

▣ "the Holy One of Israel" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE

verses.zh: 你辱骂谁，亵渎谁？扬起声来，高举眼目攻击谁呢？乃是攻击以色列的圣者。
verses.en: “‘Whom have you taunted and hurled insults at?At whom have you shoutedand looked so arrogantly?[NOTE:1] At the Holy One of Israel![NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and lifted your eyes on high?” Cf. NIV “lifted your eyes in pride”; NRSV “haughtily lifted your eyes.”
See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in 1:4.

verses.zh: 你藉你的臣仆辱骂主说：我率领许多战车上山顶，到黎巴嫩极深之处；我要砍伐其中高大的香柏树和佳美的松树。我必上极高之处，进入肥田的树林。
verses.en: Through your messengers you taunted the Lord,[NOTE:1] “With my many chariots I climbed upthe high mountains,the slopes of Lebanon.I cut down its tall cedarsand its best evergreens.I invaded its remotest regions,[NOTE:2] its thickest woods.
notes: The Hebrew term translated “Lord” here is אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay).
Heb “the height of its extremity”; ASV “its farthest height.”

verses.zh: 我已经挖井喝水；我必用脚掌踏干埃及的一切河。
verses.en: I dug wellsand drank water.[NOTE:1] With the soles of my feet I dried upall the rivers of Egypt.”’
notes: The Hebrew text has simply, “I dug and drank water.” But the parallel text in 2 Kgs 19:24 has “foreign waters.” זָרִים (zarim, “foreign”) may have accidentally dropped out of the Isaianic text by homoioteleuton (cf. NCV, NIV, NLT). Note that the preceding word, מַיִם (mayim, “water) also ends in mem (ם). The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has “foreign waters” for this line. However, in several other passages the 1QIsaa scroll harmonizes with 2 Kgs 19 against the MT (Isa 36:5; 37:9, 20). Since the addition of “foreign” to this text in Isaiah by a later scribe would be more likely than its deletion, the MT reading should be accepted.
verses.commentary:
37:25-29 At this point the focus turns from Assyria's accomplishments (although it is possible that
Isa. 37:25 refers to the arrogant claims of Sennacherib, but Isa. 37:26 cannot) to YHWH's accomplishments.

- Isa. 37:25, YHWH's control of water (i.e. life, cf. Isa. 11:15; 44:27; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS)

- Isa. 37:26-27, YHWH's ancient plans to use Assyria to punish His people (cf. Isa. 10:5). Isa. 37:27
refers to Israel and Judah's humiliation and defeat.

- Isa. 37:28, YHWH's foreknowledge (very similar to Psalm 139)

- Isa. 37:29, the consequences of arrogance against YHWH

- put a hook in your nose

- put a bridle in your lips (these are images for exile)

- turn you back by the way which you came (cf. Isa. 37:37)

verses.zh: 耶和华说：你岂没有听见我早先所做的、古时所立的吗？现在藉你使坚固城荒废，变为乱堆。
verses.en: [NOTE:1] “Certainly you must have heard![NOTE:2] Long ago I worked it out,in ancient times I planned[NOTE:3] it,and now I am bringing it to pass.The plan is this:Fortified cities will crashinto heaps of ruins.[NOTE:4]
notes: Having quoted the Assyrian king’s arrogant words in vv. 23-24, the Lord now speaks to the king.
Heb “Have you not heard?” The rhetorical question expresses the Lord’s amazement that anyone might be ignorant of what he is about to say.
Heb “formed” (so KJV, ASV).

Heb “and it is to cause to crash into heaps of ruins fortified cities.” The subject of the third feminine singular verb תְהִי (tehi) is the implied plan, referred to in the preceding lines with third feminine singular pronominal suffixes.
verses.commentary:
37:26 "Have you not heard?

Long ago I did it,

From ancient times I planned it"

This shows that God has always had a plan for dealing, not only with Assyria (10:5; Jer. 18:11;
see full note at Isa. 12:5), but also with the entire world (cf. Isa. 14:24,26; 22:11; 25:1; 46:10-11; see
full note at Isa. 12:5). History is not moving in a haphazard manner, but is on a teleological track to
an end-time confrontation and restoration.

The word translated "long ago" (BDB 935) can refer to time or space. It also can refer to

- long past time, here

- future time, cf. 2 Sam. 7:19; 1 Chr. 17:17

verses.zh: 所以其中的居民力量甚小，惊惶羞愧。他们像野草，像青菜，如房顶上的草，又如田间未长成的禾稼。
verses.en: Their residents are powerless;[NOTE:1] they are terrified and ashamed.They are as short-lived as plants in the fieldor green vegetation.[NOTE:2] They are as short-lived as grass on the rooftops[NOTE:3] when it is scorched by the east wind.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “short of hand”; KJV, ASV “of small power”; NASB “short of strength.”
Heb “they are plants in the field and green vegetation.” The metaphor emphasizes how short-lived these seemingly powerful cities really were. See Ps 90:5-6; Isa 40:6-8, 24.
Heb “[they are] grass on the rooftops.” See the preceding note.

The Hebrew text has “scorched before the standing grain” (perhaps meaning “before it reaches maturity”), but it is preferable to emend קָמָה (qamah, “standing grain”) to קָדִים (qadim, “east wind”) with the support of 1Q Isaa; cf. J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:657, n. 8.

verses.zh: 你坐下，你出去，你进来，你向我发烈怒，我都知道。
verses.en: I know where you liveand everything you doand how you rage against me.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “your going out and your coming in and how you have raged against me.” Several scholars have suggested that this line is probably dittographic (note the beginning of the next line). However, most English translations include the statement in question at the end of v. 28 and the beginning of v. 29. Interestingly, the LXX does not have this clause at the end of v. 28 and the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa does not have it at the beginning of v. 29. In light of this ambiguous manuscript evidence, it appears best to retain the clause in both verses.
verses.commentary:
37:28 "your raging against Me" This VERB (BDB 919, KB 1182,
Hithpael INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) is repeated in Isa. 37:29. Notice
the personal element!

This VERB in the Hiphil stem is often used of

- fear and trembling (cf. Isa. 14:16; 23:11)

- eschatological events (cf. Isa. 13:13)

- YHWH Himself in Ezek. 16:43

verses.zh: 因你向我发烈怒，又因你狂傲的话达到我耳中，我就要用钩子钩上你的鼻子，把嚼环放在你口里，使你从原路转回去。
verses.en: Because you rage against meand the uproar you create has reached my ears,[NOTE:1] I will put my hook in your nose,[NOTE:2] and my bit between your lips,and I will lead you back the way you came.
notes: Heb “and your complacency comes up into my ears.” The parallelism is improved if שַׁאֲנַנְךָ (shaʾananekha, “your complacency”) is emended to שְׁאוֹנְךָ (sheʾonekha, “your uproar”). See M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 237-38. However, the LXX seems to support the MT, and Sennacherib’s cavalier dismissal of Yahweh depicts an arrogant complacency (J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah [NICOT], 1:658, n. 10).
The word-picture has a parallel in Assyrian sculpture. See M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 238.
verses.commentary:
37:29 "I will put My hook in your nose" This is exactly what Assyria did to others. She tried to
frighten them by boasting of the cruelty that she had done to other nations. She tied the conquered
people together using hooks in their noses, lips, or tongues and marched them into exile (cf. 2 Kgs. 19:28).
YHWH will now do the same thing to them.

verses.zh: 「以色列人哪，我赐你们一个证据：你们今年要吃自生的，明年也要吃自长的，至于后年，你们要耕种收割，栽植葡萄园，吃其中的果子。
verses.en: [NOTE:1] “This will be your reminder that I have spoken the truth:[NOTE:2] This year you will eat what grows wild,[NOTE:3] and next year[NOTE:4] what grows on its own. But the year after that[NOTE:5] you will plant seed and harvest crops; you will plant vines and consume their produce.[NOTE:6]
notes: At this point the word concerning the king of Assyria (vv. 22-29) ends, and the Lord again addresses Hezekiah and the people directly (see v. 21).

Heb “and this is your sign.” In this case the אוֹת (ʾot, “sign”) is a future reminder of God’s intervention designated before the actual intervention takes place. For similar “signs” see Exod 3:12 and Isa 7:14-25.
This refers to crops that grew up on their own (that is, without cultivation) from the seed planted in past years.
Heb “and in the second year” (so ASV).
Heb “in the third year” (so KJV, NAB).
The four plural imperatival verb forms in v. 30b are used rhetorically. The Lord commands the people to plant, harvest, etc. to emphasize the certainty of restored peace and prosperity.
verses.commentary:
37:30 "this shall be the sign for you" This is important because Hezekiah is the Messianic
representative (i.e. a Davidic king, Isa. 7:14-16) as Ahaz was (i.e. cf. Isa. 8:8c,10c). God will show him a
sign (BDB 16) here and in Isa. 38:7 (as He did Ahaz in Isa. 7:14). This particular sign is related to a
three-year promise of full restoration of the land of Judah. I think Isa. 37:30-32 should be a separate
paragraph, as should Isa. 37:33-35 and 36-38.

Verse 30 has a series of IMPERATIVES as YHWH promises a
three-year restoration (i.e. the covenant promises of Deuteronomy 27-28).

- eat ‒ BDB 37, KB 46, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE. This
form is repeated in this verse (kethib), but the MT scholars suggested a
change (Qere) to a Qal IMPERATIVE, which
matches the other IMPERATIVES in the verse. The difference
is very close.

- ואכול, MT

- ואכלו, suggested change

- sow ‒ BDB 281, KB 282, Qal IMPERATIVE

- reap ‒ BDB 894, KB 1126, Qal IMPERATIVE

- plant ‒ BDB 642, KB 694, Qal IMPERATIVE

- eat, Qere, see note at #1, b

Just one added thought, it is possible that this promised restoration is related to
the "Year of Jubilee," Lev. 25:10, see James M. Freeman, Manners and Customs of the Bible, p. 96.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEASTS OF ISRAEL, II. C.

▣ For "sign" see
SPECIAL TOPIC: SIGN (OT)

verses.zh: 犹大家所逃脱余剩的，仍要往下扎根，向上结果。
verses.en: Those who remain in Judah will take root in the ground and bear fruit.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “The remnant of the house of Judah that is left will add roots below and produce fruit above.”
verses.commentary:
37:31 "the surviving remnant" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT, Three Senses.

▣ The agricultural imagery continues. Judah is described as

- taking a strong root

- bearing fruit

verses.zh: 必有余剩的民从耶路撒冷而出；必有逃脱的人从锡安山而来。万军之耶和华的热心必成就这事。
verses.en: “For a remnant will leave Jerusalem; survivors will come out of Mount Zion.The zeal of the Lord of Heaven’s Armies[NOTE:1] will accomplish this.
notes: Traditionally, “the Lord of hosts.” In this context the Lord’s “zeal” refers to his intense devotion to and love for his people that prompts him to protect and restore them.
verses.commentary:
37:32 Those who survive Assyria's attack will do so, not by their own plans or provisions, but
by the zeal (cf. Isa. 9:7; 59:17) of the Lord of hosts! Ahaz planned, but
Hezekiah trusted!

▣ "The zeal of the Lord of hosts" This (BDB 888) refers to YHWH's special love
and care for His covenant people (a faithless wife of Hosea 1-3). YHWH acts passionately for His purposes
in redemption (cf. Isa. 63:15-19, which involves the children of Abraham, cf. Gen. 12:1-3). The phrase
has Messianic implications in Isa. 9:7 and 59:17. Context determines whether (1) zealous or (2) jealous
is the best translation. The term can have either a positive or negative connotation depending on the
context. Here it is surely positive and redemptive!

SPECIAL TOPIC: JEALOUSY, ZEAL (NOUN)

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts

verses.zh: 「所以耶和华论亚述王如此说：他必不得来到这城，也不在这里射箭，不得拿盾牌到城前，也不筑垒攻城。
verses.en: “So this is what the Lord says about the king of Assyria: “‘He will not enter this city,nor will he shoot an arrow here.[NOTE:1] He will not attack it with his shielded warriors,[NOTE:2] nor will he build siege works against it.
notes: Heb “there” (so KJV, NASB, NRSV). In terms of English style “here” is expected in collocation with “this” in the previous line.
Heb “[with] a shield” (so ASV, NASB, NRSV).
verses.commentary:
37:33-34 This is a promise that no siege will occur against Jerusalem. At this point the Assyrian
army was not before the gates of Jerusalem, but still at walled cities of the Shephelah some distance away,
such as Lachish.

There are several things that YHWH will allow and not allow in relation to Assyria's attack
on Jerusalem.

- the army of Assyria shall not come to Jerusalem to besiege it

- the army shall not shoot an arrow there

- the army shall not come with shield

- the army shall not throw up a siege mound

- Assyria shall retreat the way she came

verses.zh: 他从哪条路来，必从那条路回去，必不得来到这城。这是耶和华说的。
verses.en: He will go back the way he came—he will not enter this city,’ says the Lord.

verses.zh: 因我为自己的缘故，又为我仆人大卫的缘故，必保护拯救这城。」
verses.en: I will shield this city and rescue it for the sake of my reputation and because of my promise to David my servant.”[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “for my sake and for the sake of David my servant.”
verses.commentary:
37:35 The reason given for Assyria's limitations and retreat are

- YHWH Himself will defend (BDB 170, KB 199, Qal PERFECT with waw) the
city (i.e. Holy War imagery, cf. 2 Kgs. 19:34)

- YHWH will deliver/save it (BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil
INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)

- YHWH does it

- for Himself (i.e. His eternal redemptive plan and His personal reputation, cf. Ezek. 36:22-38)

- for His servant David (cf. Isa. 9:7; 11:1; 16:5; 22:9,22; 29:1; 38:5; 55:3; 2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

verses.zh: 耶和华的使者出去，在亚述营中杀了十八万五千人。清早有人起来一看，都是死尸了。
verses.en: The angel of the Lord went out and killed 185,000 troops[NOTE:1] in the Assyrian camp. When they[NOTE:2] got up early the next morning, there were all the corpses![NOTE:3]
notes: The word “troops” is supplied in the translation for smoothness and clarity.
This refers to the Israelites and/or the rest of the Assyrian army.
Heb “look, all of them were dead bodies”; NLT “they found corpses everywhere.”
verses.commentary:
37:36 "the angel of the Lord went out" This is similar to the personage of
the death angel who represented YHWH's presence in the last plague on Egypt in Exodus 11 and 12:23,29
(also note 2 Sam. 24:16).

There is no "grim reaper." YHWH controls life and death. It is hard to separate the
sovereignty of God from conditions of a fallen world. This is not the world that God intended it to be.
Death is the result of human rebellion. God knows, allows, and executes His will. Secondary causes,
so important to us, were not part of the ancient worldview (i.e. Matt. 6:25-27; 10:28-31), where there
was no distinction between the supernatural and natural.

For full notes on "one causality" see note at Isa. 14:24-27.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ANGEL OF THE LORD

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

▣ "struck 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians" This was not before the walls of Jerusalem, but
apparently some distance away at the Assyrian camp (cf. 2 Kgs. 19:35). Herodotus, an ancient historian,
records this plague and implies that it was related to rodents, possibly bubonic plague. This judgment did
not kill the entire army. This very event is foreshadowed in Isa. 31:8, where it is described as death by
the sword of the Lord. However, here it seems to be a plague.

Remember, this is hyperbolic poetry, not historical narrative. Modern western readers are
unduly affected by their own worldviews and read the Bible (an ancient eastern book) through the filter
of their current understanding of history and literature, which always causes confusion and misunderstanding!
See "Bible Interpretation Seminar".

verses.zh: 亚述王西拿基立就拔营回去，住在尼尼微。
verses.en: So King Sennacherib of Assyria broke camp and went on his way. He went home and stayed in Nineveh.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and went and returned and lived in Nineveh.”
verses.commentary: 37:37 "Nineveh" This was the capital of Assyria and was located on the Tigris River.

verses.zh: 一日在他的神―尼斯洛庙里叩拜，他儿子亚得米勒和沙利色用刀杀了他，就逃到亚拉腊地。他儿子以撒哈顿接续他作王。
verses.en: One day,[NOTE:1] as he was worshiping[NOTE:2] in the temple of his god Nisroch,[NOTE:3] his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him down with the sword.[NOTE:4] They ran away to the land of Ararat; his son Esarhaddon replaced him as king.
notes: The assassination of King Sennacherib probably took place in 681 b.c.
The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.

No such Mesopotamian god is presently known. Perhaps the name Nisroch is a textual variation of Nusku, the Mesopotamian god of light and fire. Other proposals have tried to relate the name to Ashur, the chief god of the Assyria, or to Ninurta, the Assyrian god of war.
Extra-biblical sources also mention the assassination of Sennacherib, though they refer to only one assassin. See M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 239-40.
verses.commentary:
37:38 "Nisroch his god" This is an unknown name.

- The LXX translation of this is a spelling very similar to the god of the city of Asshur, who was
the head of the Assyrian pantheon.

- It is also possible that it is a misspelling of "Nusku" (BDB 652;
NET footnote), the Babylonian and Assyrian god
of light and fire who was worshiped at Haran and associated with the moon god (i.e. his son).

- E. J. Young thinks it was an intentional corruption of the name Marduk. See James M. Freeman,
Manners and Customs of the Bible, p. 182.

We know from historical documentation that there is a twenty-year gap between Isa. 37:37 and 38.
This prophecy was literally fulfilled in 681 B.C. when Sennacherib's two sons
assassinated him and the third son took the throne.

681-669 B.C.

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Isaiah 37:1-7 describes the reactions of Hezekiah to the Assyrian message in Isaiah 36.

- It is uncertain if Isa. 37:1-7 and 14-20 are two separate reactions. It seems contextually that
after Isa. 37:8-9 Sennacherib sent a second message to be delivered to Jerusalem and Isa. 37:14-20
are Hezekiah's response to this second message, which is similar to the first one.

Possibly Hezekiah was trusting YHWH and Egypt in Isa. 37:1-7, but after Isa. 37:9 he
had to trust YHWH alone (cf. Isa. 37:14-20,30).
